clue.text: The complaint is about an alien letter, or word, being obstinately retained

parts.note: mumps is a familiar childhood illness, a complaint

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: taken as written
mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet, foreign to English

explanation.surface: A doctor's note about a patient fixated on a strange foreign letter or word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alien letter' points to the Greek alphabet. 'or' joins the wordplay to the definition: a mumpsimus is a mistaken word a person refuses to give up.
explanation.definitionFit: A mumpsimus is an error, or a mistaken expression, that someone clings to stubbornly even after correction.

clue.text: A play to take the mickey out of King Claudius?

definitions.text: A play to take the mickey out of King Claudius?

parts.words: A play to take the mickey out of King Claudius?
parts.note: Hamlet stages a play to catch his uncle King Claudius's guilt; a trap removes a mouse such as Mickey

explanation.surface: A stage satire mocking King Claudius.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take the mickey' means mock, but here a Mickey is a mouse caught. Hamlet names his play-within-the-play after this device.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's play within the play bears this name, as does a mouse-catching device.

clue.text: Choral work from books found in the Opera House

indicators.note: found in means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: the Met is New York's Metropolitan Opera House
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Sheet music for a choir taken from books in the opera house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short sacred composition for unaccompanied voices.

clue.text: An MP is twice treated to a mustard plaster

indicators.note: treated means the letters are processed and rearranged
twice means the word is is used two times

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician given an old-fashioned mustard poultice twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' rearranges AN, MP, IS and IS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinapism is a medical poultice made with ground mustard seed.

clue.text: Italian family on new vitamin cure

parts.note: the Medici were the ruling family of Renaissance Florence
E is a vitamin

explanation.surface: An Italian dynasty adopting a new vitamin remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' simply joins the pieces, MEDICI above N and E in a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Medicine is a remedy, something taken to treat illness.

clue.text: Possessed gilt-edged protection

indicators.note: edged means the first word forms a border on each side of the second

parts.note: a gilt is a young female pig, which becomes a sow
had means possessed

explanation.surface: Owning a safe gilt-edged investment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gilt-edged' suggests safe stocks and shares. Split, a gilt is a young female pig, and 'edged' tells you the pig's grown-up name goes round the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A shadow can mean shelter or protection, as in under the shadow of one's wing.

clue.text: Metal that's extracted from wood

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Metal that's extracted from wood' (5) for BRASS: no parse found linking wood to BRASS; neither scan nor search gives the setter's mechanism

clue.text: Kipling poem about English wagoner

indicators.note: about means the poem's title goes round the other piece

parts.note: Boots is Kipling's marching poem from Barrack-Room Ballads

explanation.surface: A Kipling poem about an English carter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootes is the constellation called the Herdsman or Wagoner, driving the Plough.

clue.text: After line-out, handsome youth wins point from defender

indicators.note: wins means the first piece gains the next one added on
out means the letter for line is removed

parts.note: Apollo is the Greek god famed for youthful beauty
the gist is the main point

explanation.surface: A rugby lineout where a handsome youngster scores a point off a defender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'line-out' looks like rugby but tells you to drop an L from APOLLO, giving APOLO, which 'wins' GIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologist argues in defence of a belief or cause.

clue.text: Sword, we hear, from this monumental stone

indicators.note: we hear means the word for sword is said aloud

parts.note: steel is a poetic word for a sword

explanation.surface: A sword drawn from a monument, like Excalibur from the stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A stele is an upright stone slab bearing an inscription, a monument.

clue.text: Like sweet bells jangled, or an inefficient engine

definitions.meaning: Ophelia in Hamlet describes Hamlet's mind as sweet bells jangled, out of tune and harsh
an engine that has not been adjusted for best running wastes fuel

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare set beside a badly running car.
explanation.definitionFit: Bells out of harmony and a motor never given its tune-up are both lacking adjustment.

clue.text: Removal of the finale in cinema, for example

definitions.text: Removal of the finale in cinema, for example

parts.words: Removal of the finale in cinema, for example
parts.note: the word cinema is a clipped form of cinematograph, its ending cut off; the clue reads like the last reel of a film being cut

explanation.surface: A film being shown with its final scene cut.
explanation.definitionFit: The linguistic term for dropping the last sound or syllable of a word, as cinematograph became cinema.

clue.text: Return cups to end of the bar

indicators.note: end of picks out the final letter of the word the
return means the word for cups is read backwards

parts.note: pots are cups or trophies

explanation.surface: A barman being told to bring the cups back to the end of the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' signals reading the word for cups backwards. 'bar' looks like a pub counter but is a legal verb, to preclude.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to estop is to preclude or prevent someone from making a claim.

clue.text: Shotgun — one way to silence the club menace

parts.note: to choke someone off is to silence them
the club bore is the tedious member everyone avoids

explanation.surface: Shooting the club's most boring member as a way of shutting him up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one way to' is a link between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A choke-bore is a shotgun whose barrel narrows towards the muzzle to tighten the spread of shot.

clue.text: Eat one's words about America refusing to submit to authority

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: to eat one's words is to take back a statement, to recant
US is the United States, America

explanation.surface: Someone retracting statements about the USA while defying authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' tells you to put America inside the word for taking back what you said. 'Eat one's words' is an idiom, not food.
explanation.definitionFit: Recusant historically described Catholics refusing Church of England services; generally it means defying authority.

clue.text: Business at the Old Bailey temporarily suspended 'for lack of: bottle

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Business at the Old Bailey temporarily suspended for lack of bottle' (9) for COWARDICE: ON ICE and CO are clear but no reading of 'at the Old Bailey' as WARD was found or confirmed by search
annotationWithheld.clue: Business at the Old Bailey temporarily suspended 'for lack of: bottle

clue.text: In a hazardous position out on this mountain spur

definitions.text: In a hazardous position out on this
definitions.meaning: to be in a risky, exposed position
a ... can be a projecting spur or offshoot of a mountain range

explanation.surface: A climber in danger out on a mountain spur.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom out on a limb completes the first sense; a branching ridge from a hill is the second.

clue.text: The absence of this sinister strawberry reunited long-lost brothers

definitions.text: The absence of this sinister strawberry reunited long-lost brothers

parts.words: The absence of this sinister strawberry reunited long-lost brothers
parts.note: in melodrama, siblings are recognised by a strawberry-shaped mark on the skin; here its absence twists the cliche

explanation.surface: A melodrama in which brothers find each other through a missing family mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strawberry' is not a fruit but a red mark on the skin; 'sinister' can mean on the left.
explanation.definitionFit: A strawberry mark on the skin from infancy is the classic token of identity in Victorian melodrama.

clue.text: Matilda in glad rags for dance

indicators.note: in means the first piece is placed inside the other
rags means the word glad is torn up and rearranged

parts.note: Belloc's cautionary tale is about Matilda, who told lies, so she is a liar

explanation.surface: A girl in her finery for a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilaire Belloc's cautionary verse tells of Matilda, who told such dreadful lies; 'rags' scrambles the word glad, and 'in' puts her vice inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The galliard is a lively Renaissance court dance in triple time.

clue.text: Grandson who deflected Isaac's right hand

indicators.note: deflected means turned aside, so these letters are redirected into a new order

explanation.surface: A grandson who knocked aside his grandfather's right hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deflected' rearranges ISAACS with R and H. Genesis tells of Jacob blessing his grandsons with crossed hands, which the surface echoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Issachar was a son of Jacob and therefore a grandson of Isaac.

clue.text: Sound of boy making a catch

indicators.note: sound of means the word for boy is said aloud

parts.note: Paul is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A boy who makes a catch at cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' is a link. A pawl is a pivoted bar that engages a ratchet.
explanation.definitionFit: A pawl is a mechanical catch that stops a ratchet wheel from turning backwards.

clue.text: Gargantua in 'conversation giving a bit of cheek

indicators.note: in conversation means the phrase is spoken, so its sound is used

parts.note: Rabelais's giant Gargantua was famed for prodigious eating, a mass eater

explanation.surface: Rabelais's giant chatting and being cheeky.
explanation.walkthrough: Gargantua is Rabelais's giant with a vast appetite; spoken, mass eater sounds like the muscle's name. The stray quotation mark is from the page.
explanation.definitionFit: The masseter is the jaw muscle in the cheek used for chewing, so it is a part of the face.

clue.text: Secret many patent

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a large number
patent means obvious or overt

explanation.surface: A hidden numerous set of patents.
explanation.definitionFit: Covert means hidden or concealed, done in secret.

clue.text: Noble successor, finally, to the Duke's Deputy

indicators.note: successor means the following piece comes after the first

parts.note: an angel was an old English gold coin, like the noble

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word to

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's heir becoming the Duke's deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noble' looks like a peer but is a coin, the ANGEL. Angelo is the Duke's deputy in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure.
explanation.definitionFit: In Measure for Measure, the Duke leaves Angelo to govern Vienna in his place.

clue.text: Use force to put half-nelson on someone

indicators.note: on means the first piece comes after the other in an across answer

parts.note: a person is someone

indicators.note: half here asks for the first half of the word nelson, its opening three letters

explanation.surface: A wrestler using force to put a half-nelson on an opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-nelson' looks like a wrestling hold, but split it gives the halving signal and the name. 'Use' and 'to put' are joining words, and 'force' means a workforce.
explanation.definitionFit: A workforce or body of staff is its personnel.

clue.text: Fold in the sample attached

indicators.note: in the means the letters are found running inside the following words

explanation.surface: A fabric sample with a crease pinned to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is a double fold pressed into cloth.

clue.text: Stupid bull, first for the hecatomb

parts.note: Apis was the sacred bull worshipped in ancient Egypt

indicators.note: first for the means take the opening letter of the word hecatomb

explanation.surface: A dim bull is the first to be sacrificed in a great offering.
explanation.walkthrough: A hecatomb is a sacrifice of many cattle, so the bull sits in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Apish means silly or foolishly imitative, like a monkey.

clue.text: I hear a joiner in the house

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: hear means the word for a joiner is taken by its sound

parts.note: glue joins things together

explanation.surface: A carpenter working in a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joiner' suggests a carpenter, but it is glue. 'in the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is an Inuit dome dwelling built of snow blocks.

clue.text: Play the dumb blonde, perhaps, or this more ambiguous figure

definitions.meaning: Ben Jonson's comedy is subtitled The Silent Woman; a dumb blonde is a silent woman, perhaps
someone of indeterminate sex, sharing traits of both

explanation.surface: An actor playing a dizzy blonde, or a more ambiguous character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dumb' means silent here, not stupid, leading to Jonson's play Epicoene, or The Silent Woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonson's play title also names an androgynous, sexless person.

clue.text: The least sunny parts of our annual trips to see Herbert Lamb

definitions.text: The least sunny parts of our annual trips

parts.note: A P Herbert, the humorist, signed his Punch pieces with his initials APH
Charles Lamb wrote his essays under the pen name Elia

explanation.surface: A holiday spent visiting two literary figures on the least sunny trips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'our annual trips' are the Earth's orbits round the Sun; 'to see' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphelia are the points in an orbit farthest from the Sun, so least sunny.

clue.text: Taking the front end, try the weight

indicators.note: front end picks out the opening letter of the word the

parts.note: to heft something is to lift it to judge how heavy it is

explanation.surface: Lifting the front end of something to gauge its weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking what is not yours is stealing.

clue.text: Where one may go through the motions of class work

definitions.text: Where one may go through the motions

parts.note: an order is a class or rank
a book is a written work

explanation.surface: A pupil just going through the motions of classwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'motions' are the parliamentary kind, listed in the Order Book of the House of Commons; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Commons order book lists motions and questions for debate, where business is gone through.
